corpus_definition: To end a phone conversation by putting the receiver down.
particle_note: Usually used without an object: 'He hung up.' 'Hang up the phone' or 'hang the phone up' is also possible. 'Hang up on someone' = end the call suddenly while they are still talking.

relations.note: Easy everyday phrase with the same idea.
Plain and clear; common with mobile phones.
To answer the phone and start talking.
To start a phone call when it rings; hang up is how a call ends.

context.text: My grandmother always hangs up before I can say goodbye. Yesterday I called her back and laughed, 'Please don't hang up on me again!'

reviewer_note: Only the phone meaning; 'hang up clothes' (put on a hook) is a different meaning and is not used here.

corpus_definition: a very strong feeling of dislike for someone

forms.definition: a very strong feeling of dislike or anger toward someone
forms.example: His hatred of injustice made him become a lawyer.

syn.note: Very close; a strong and more literary word.
Unfriendly feelings or behaviour, often between groups or countries.
Easy word, but much weaker: you can dislike something without strong feelings.
Anger can be short; hatred usually lasts a long time.

ant.note: A strong warm feeling for someone.
A gentle feeling of liking and caring for someone.

forms.definition: to dislike someone or something very much
forms.example: I hate waiting for the bus in the rain.
forms.note: Hate is also a noun with almost the same meaning as hatred: 'full of hate'.

syn.note: Very strong and a little formal.
Very strong; often about people or food.
Easy, informal phrase: 'I can't stand loud music.'
Much weaker; you just don't like it.

ant.note: To like someone or something very much.
To enjoy or think something is nice.

forms.definition: very unkind and unpleasant, showing strong dislike
forms.example: He said some hateful things to his neighbour.

syn.note: Easy word for very unkind or unpleasant.
Wanting to hurt or upset someone.
Cruel is about causing pain on purpose.

ant.note: Friendly and caring.
Showing warm feelings for someone.

forms.note: There is no common adverb. 'Hatefully' exists but is very rare; learners say 'with hatred'.

people.definition: a person who often says bad things about others, especially online
people.example: Don't worry about one hater in the comments; your video is great.

context.text: Hatred between the two families lasted for many years. Now their children say they don't hate anyone; they just want to play football together.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR B1). -red in hatred is not a transparent learner affix, so no affix is claimed for it.

corpus_definition: to be wearing a piece of clothing.
particle_note: Separable and usually split: 'She had a red hat on.' Not used in continuous forms: say 'He has a coat on', not 'He is having a coat on'. In British English 'have got on' is also common.

relations.note: Same meaning and more common in writing: 'She was wearing a red hat.'
Often used to describe all of someone's clothes.
To remove clothes; after you take off a coat, you no longer have it on.

context.text: It was cold, but Aziz only had a T-shirt on. His mother asked, 'Why don't you have your warm jacket on?'

reviewer_note: Stative phrasal verb: warned against continuous use. Not the 'trick someone' meaning (have someone on).

corpus_definition: The main title of a news story.

forms.definition: the title printed in large letters above a news story
forms.example: I read the headline in the newspaper.
forms.note: 'The headlines' can also mean the most important news on TV or radio.

syn.note: Title is general (books, films); a headline is for news.
A title at the top of a page or part of a text.
Words under a photo, not above a story.

forms.definition: to give a news story a particular title
forms.example: The story was headlined 'Heat wave hits Tashkent'.
forms.note: Usually passive. It also means 'to be the main performer at a concert'.

syn.note: To give something a name; used for books, songs and articles.

forms.note: No adjective. 'Headline' is used before a noun instead: 'headline news'.

people.definition: the main and most famous performer at a concert or festival
people.example: The headliner came on stage at ten o'clock.
people.note: Belongs to headline = be the main act at a show, not a news title.

context.text: Did you see the headline this morning? The story was headlined 'New metro line opens in Tashkent', and everyone on the bus was talking about it.

reviewer_note: Headline is itself a compound (head + line), so no affix is claimed; headliner is the concert meaning.

corpus_definition: The back rounded part of the bottom of a foot.

forms.definition: the round back part of your foot, under the ankle
forms.example: Her heel was sore from wearing uncomfortable shoes.
forms.note: It also means the raised back part of a shoe: 'shoes with high heels'.

syn.note: The heel is one part of the foot.
The whole bottom of the foot or shoe.

ant.note: Toes are at the front of the foot; the heel is at the back.

forms.definition: of a dog, to walk close behind its owner
forms.example: The dog heeled when the farmer called it.
forms.note: Belongs to heel = staying at someone's heels; mostly used as a command to a dog: 'Heel!'
Only compounds such as high-heeled and well-heeled (rich); these go to the Compounds branch.

context.text: My new shoes hurt my heel on the walk to school. Tonight I will put a plaster on both heels.

reviewer_note: Body meaning only; shoe heel mentioned in a note. Compounds (high-heeled) left out.

corpus_definition: to pause because you are not sure what to do or say

forms.definition: a short pause because you are not sure
forms.example: She answered the question without hesitation.

syn.note: Easy word for a short stop; it doesn't always mean you are unsure.
The feeling of not being sure.
The state of not being sure about something.
Something happens later than planned.

ant.note: The feeling of being sure about what you do.

forms.definition: the feeling of being unsure and slow to act
forms.example: There was some hesitancy among parents about the new school rules.

forms.definition: to stop for a moment because you are not sure
forms.example: She hesitated before answering the difficult question.
forms.note: Common in polite phrases: 'Don't hesitate to call me.'

syn.note: Stop for a short time; easy and common.
Not do something because you are unsure or afraid.
Be unable to decide between two things.
Wait is general; it doesn't mean you are unsure.

forms.definition: slow to do or say something because you are unsure
forms.example: He was hesitant to ask the teacher for help.

syn.note: Easy word: not certain.
Not sure what to do or believe.
Not wanting to do something, not only unsure.
Not sure that something is true or good.

ant.note: Sure of yourself and your actions.
Certain about what to do.

forms.definition: in a slow way that shows you are not sure
forms.example: She smiled hesitantly at the new students.

syn.note: In a way that shows you are not sure.
Easy word, but only about speed.

ant.note: In a way that shows you are sure.

context.text: Don't hesitate to ask questions in class. Last year I was hesitant to speak English, but now I answer without hesitation.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged (lowest CEFR B1). -ant in hesitant not claimed as an affix (no clean English base).

corpus_definition: A small piece of information that helps you guess something.

forms.definition: a small piece of information that helps you guess
forms.example: She gave me a hint about my surprise party.
forms.note: It can also mean a useful tip ('cooking hints') or a very small amount ('a hint of lemon').

syn.note: Almost the same; very common in games and puzzles.
Something that shows what is true or will happen.
An idea someone gives you, often more direct.
A piece of useful advice, not help to guess.

forms.definition: to say something in an indirect way so others can guess
forms.example: She hinted that she wanted a new phone for her birthday.
forms.note: Patterns: hint that + clause; hint at something.

syn.note: Easy and common; can be direct or indirect.
More formal: show something without saying it.
Show that something is true; often formal.

context.text: My sister wouldn't tell me about my present, but she gave me a hint: it's something to read. Later she hinted that it was by an Uzbek writer.

reviewer_note: Noun meaning 'clue'; the 'small amount' and 'tip' uses are in a note only.

corpus_definition: The quality of always speaking the truth to other people.

forms.definition: the quality of always telling the truth and not cheating
forms.example: Honesty is the most important part of our friendship.

syn.note: Almost the same, but less common.
Meaning what you say and feel.
Saying what you think openly, even if it is not nice.
Having strong moral rules and following them.

ant.note: Lying, cheating or stealing.
Trying to make people believe something false.

forms.definition: always telling the truth and never cheating
forms.example: Thank you for your honest answer.

syn.note: Telling the truth.
Really meaning what you say.
Saying what you think directly.
Treating people equally; easy word.

ant.note: Lying or cheating.

forms.definition: in a truthful way, without lying or cheating
forms.example: Please answer all the questions honestly.
forms.note: Also used to show you mean what you say: 'Honestly, I don't know.'

syn.note: In a way that tells the truth.
Really meaning it.
Openly and directly.

ant.note: In a way that involves lying or cheating.

context.text: Our teacher says honesty matters more than marks. If you answer honestly, people will see that you are an honest person.

reviewer_note: Headword is the noun; honest is its base. Negative forms (dishonest, dishonesty) kept in ant lists only.

corpus_definition: not thinking you are better or more important than others

forms.definition: the quality of not thinking you are better than others
forms.example: He accepted the prize with great humility.

syn.note: Very close; modesty is also about not talking about your success.
Living or acting in a plain, simple way.

ant.note: Feeling that you are better or more important than others.
Showing that you think you are better than others.

forms.definition: to make someone feel less important or proud
forms.example: Losing the final match humbled the team.
forms.note: Often in the passive: 'I was humbled by their kindness.'

syn.note: Make someone feel bad; stronger and more negative.
Make someone less powerful or proud.

forms.definition: not thinking you are better or more important than others
forms.example: Despite his fame, the actor remained kind and modest; he was always humble.
forms.note: It can also mean 'poor or low in rank': 'a humble home'.

syn.note: Easy and very close in meaning.
Quiet and not wanting attention.
Practical and friendly, not proud.

ant.note: Thinking you are more important than others.
Showing too clearly that you think you are better.

forms.definition: making you feel less important or proud
forms.example: Meeting the old war veterans was a humbling experience.

forms.definition: in a modest way, without feeling more important than others
forms.example: He humbly thanked everyone for their help.

syn.note: Easy and very close in meaning.

ant.note: In a way that shows you feel important.
In a way that shows you think you are better.

context.text: Our grandfather is a humble man. He talks about his success humbly and says humility is the key to a happy life.

reviewer_note: Humility is the learner-dictionary noun of humble (Latin humilis), not humbleness; 'humble = low in rank' mentioned in a note only.

corpus_definition: not allowed by the laws of a place.

forms.definition: the fact of being against the law
forms.example: The court looked at the illegality of the new building.

syn.note: An action that breaks the law; easy word.
Bad or illegal behaviour; a formal word.

ant.note: The fact of being allowed by law.

forms.note: No verb. To make something against the law we say 'ban' or 'outlaw'. The opposite family has legalize (make something allowed).

forms.definition: not allowed by the law of a country or place
forms.example: It is illegal to drive without a licence.

syn.note: Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Same meaning; formal and used in legal texts.
Officially not allowed, often by a rule, not only a law.
Not allowed by a rule, law or person.
About crime; stronger than illegal.

ant.note: Allowed by law.
Formal: allowed by law.

forms.definition: in a way that is against the law
forms.example: He parked illegally outside the school.

syn.note: Same meaning; formal.

ant.note: In a way that the law allows.

context.text: It is illegal to sell cigarettes to children in Uzbekistan. Shops that do it illegally can lose their licence.

reviewer_note: Negative-prefix headword: il- is not in the affix table, so it isn't claimed; legal/legality/legally kept as antonyms, not forms.
